group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
An 87-year-old man was escorted to the emergency department by family at dawn after they found him seated upright in his recliner, breathing rapidly and conversing in disjointed fragments about events that had taken place decades earlier; he required gentle verbal redirection before answering orientation questions and never fully grasped the exact calendar date. According to relatives, he had been in his usual state of health until three nights ago, when a dry cough surfaced and a low rumble was heard in his chest each time he exhaled. The cough turned productive of streaked rust-colored sputum yesterday afternoon, accompanied by uncontrollable shivering and a measured axillary temperature of 40.1 °C that prompted the household to place cool towels over his forehead. They deliberately withheld antipyretics, antibiotics, inhalers, and supplemental oxygen so that hospital staff could obtain an unaltered physiologic baseline. The patient resides in his own single-story home, climbs five porch steps without assistance on most mornings to fetch the newspaper, and cooks a modest breakfast daily. His medical chart lists long-standing systolic dysfunction diagnosed after an anterior myocardial infarction twenty years ago, with the last outpatient echocardiogram six months earlier noting an ejection fraction of 30 % and mild biatrial enlargement. He is followed by nephrology for stage 4 chronic kidney impairment attributed to hypertensive nephrosclerosis; baseline creatinine has hovered around 3 mg/dL with a blood urea nitrogen in the mid-40 mg/dL range, and he has not begun renal replacement therapy. There is no record of prior strokes or transient ischemic attacks, no chronic liver pathology, and no malignant diagnoses. Medications taken routinely each dawn include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg, torsemide 40 mg, and low-dose aspirin; he had ingested only these tablets with a half cup of tea three hours before arrival. He quit smoking thirty-five years earlier after a thirty-pack-year exposure, enjoys an occasional glass of whiskey on holidays, and denies recreational drug use. Immunizations are current for both pneumococcal formulations and last season’s influenza vaccine. During the thirteen-minute car ride he received no oxygen, intravenous fluids, or nebulized therapy. On arrival he sat slumped forward, eyelids half-closed, speaking in abrupt one- to two-word replies. Skin was flushed, hot, and lightly diaphoretic, with mottled patches on the knees; capillary refill was brisk. Untreated triage vitals revealed an oral temperature of 40.1 °C, irregularly regular pulse 133 beats min⁻¹, automated blood pressure 150/82 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 55 breaths min⁻¹ with nasal flaring and intercostal use, and fingertip pulse oximetry of 78 % on ambient air at this sea-level institution. Jugular venous pulsation rose 5 cm above the sternal angle while he reclined at 30°, and bilateral lower extremities showed thin, shiny skin with 1+ pitting to the mid-shin. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a rapid S1 and S2 with a faint third sound and no new murmurs. The lung examination revealed markedly diminished breath sounds over the inferior half of the right posterior thorax with stony dullness to percussion; coarse inspiratory crackles and tubular breathing were appreciated just superior to that zone, while the left lung transmitted scattered crackles without wheeze. The abdomen was soft and scaphoid with normal bowel sounds; no hepatosplenomegaly was palpable. Neurologic screening demonstrated pupils equal and reactive, but he scored only 2 of 5 points on orientation and followed two-step commands inconsistently, though motor strength appeared symmetric at 4/5 across all limbs. A bedside finger-stick glucose measured 147 mg/dL at the moment vascular access was obtained. Venous chemistries drawn within ten minutes—before any saline flushes—showed sodium 161 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 29 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 60 mg/dL, and creatinine 3.2 mg/dL. Complete blood count revealed leukocytes 18.7 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ with 91 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 65 %, hemoglobin 21.6 g/dL, and platelets 240 × 10⁹ L⁻¹. A right radial arterial sample on room air yielded pH 7.68, PaCO₂ 24 mm Hg, PaO₂ 49 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 28 mEq/L, and an alveolar-arterial gradient markedly widened for age, indicating severe hypoxemia with prominent respiratory alkalosis. Serum lactate was 2.2 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin T was below the reporting threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any therapy displayed a dense homogeneous opacity occupying the right middle and lower lobes with air bronchograms and a fluid meniscus blunting the right costophrenic angle; cardiomediastinal silhouette was mildly enlarged compared with prior films. Focused bedside ultrasound confirmed an anechoic layer tracking along the right posterior pleural surface and showed a moderately dilated left ventricle with globally reduced systolic excursion, similar to outpatient studies. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram documented atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response at 132 beats min⁻¹, unchanged QRS morphology, and no acute ischemic features. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, and urinary antigens for Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae were collected prior to any antimicrobial or vasoactive administration. Up to the completion of this note the patient remains seated upright breathing ambient air, has not received intravenous fluids, diuretics, antipyretics, bronchodilators, or supplemental oxygen, ensuring every vital sign, laboratory datum, and imaging finding above reflects his untreated presentation physiology.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and imaging points at presentation.
- Demographics: a man's baseline score is his age in years, so age 87 gives 87. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0. Subtotal: 87.
- Comorbidities: systolic heart failure +10; chronic kidney disease +10. No malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease: 0 each. Subtotal: 20.
- Examination: new disorientation +20; respiratory rate 55/min (≥30) +20; systolic BP 150 mmHg (not <90) +0; temperature 40.1 °C (<35 or ≥40) +15; pulse 133/min (≥125) +10. Subtotal: 65.
- Tests: arterial pH 7.68 (not <7.35) +0; BUN 60 mg/dL (≥30) +20; sodium 161 mEq/L (not <130) +0; glucose 147 mg/dL (not ≥250) +0; hematocrit 65% (not <30%) +0. Room-air PaO₂ 49 mmHg (<60) adds 10; the low oxygen saturation is not scored again. Right pleural effusion adds 10. Subtotal: 40.
Total PSI = 87 + 20 + 65 + 40 = 212.
Final answer: 212
